BBC News, 15 November 2026 06:32 GMT

Food firms hope EU deal will end 'onerous' export process

Abbie and Steven Williamson smile for the camera as they stand on a quayside. Abbie has long brown hair. Steven has a beard and wears glasses. Both are wearing dark blue shirts and coats.

Since Brexit, businesses exporting products including sausages and shellfish to the EU must have every consignment approved by a vet

A sausage manufacturer and a shellfish producer in the East of England say they hope a forthcoming EU summit will result in a deal to make it easier for them to sell to Europe.

The government is hoping to finalise an agreement which would remove post-Brexit checks from food and agricultural exports, meaning less paperwork and no more expensive checks.

Ministers say the deal could be worth as much as £5bn to the UK economy and could encourage businesses to grow.

But an MP who played a leading role in the Leave campaign says the proposed deal would mean the UK following EU rules again, and the government should respect the result of the referendum.

'Red tape costs an extra £32,500 a year'

Abbie and Steven Williamson run Lynn Shellfish, which sends £7.5m-worth of produce to the EU every year

In an office on the quayside at King's Lynn Docks, Abbie Williamson is preparing to do the paperwork for a shipment of cockles and whelks which will be leaving the next day for France.

About two-thirds of the catch processed by Lynn Shellfish is sold to the EU.

\"Before Brexit, it was just one piece of paperwork. Now you're looking at 10 pieces, and they take anything up to four hours to fill in,\" she says.

As part of the process, a vet has to inspect every pallet that's going on the lorry and fill out a 15-page health certificate.

With lorries going to France every few days, she says the company is spending an extra £32,500 a year on vets and customs fees.  Even then, there's no guarantee the shipment will get through.

\"We are still getting lorries rejected occasionally,\" she says.

\"We had one rejected last year because they didn't like the labels on the trays which we had been using for the last four years. The lorry had to come all the way back and we had to change the labels.\"

Shrimp being processed at Lynn Shellfish in Norfolk

The EU says the paperwork and inspections are necessary because Britain is no longer part of its regulatory framework, and it needs to be sure our food is safe.

Williamson says any deal which reduces paperwork \"would make a big difference\".

\"It would also give us the chance to enter the EU through different routes,\" she adds.

\"At the moment, we go through Boulogne because it normally works, but being able to use other ports like the Hook of Holland more easily could save time and costs.\"

Her father Steven, who runs the company, says a deal is necessary to help his industry but he feels conflicted because he voted for Brexit and any deal with the EU will almost certainly involve having to accept its rules on food production.

\"That's not what I voted for, but we need a deal,\" he says.

\"It's what's needed for my industry to have a future.

\"Too many companies have suffered because of Brexit. We were promised the earth and were delivered nothing.\"

Jonathan Edge says reduced paperwork could allow him to expand and employ more people

Jonathan Edge runs Broad Oak Farm Sausage Company in Essex – a family business in Hatfield Broad Oak, near Bishop's Stortford, that employs 50 people.

It sells about £130,000-worth of sausages to the EU every year, which is just 7% of its total produce. But the paperwork involved in getting them there takes up a large proportion of his staff's time.

\"Since Brexit, it has gone from something that was quite a simple process involving a very basic shipping document [to] quite an onerous process involving health certificates and veterinary inspections of every consignment,\" he says.

\"We were already exporting to the Far East and the Caribbean so it was more of the same for us, but for a company that hasn't done anything like this before, Brexit was a huge, huge change.\"

Sausage production at Broad Oak Farm Sausage Company

He sees the proposed agreement as a potential opportunity for small and medium-size firms such as his.

\"It would reduce our costs, and if it went back to the simple process it was before Brexit,  it would encourage you to push yourself and grow your exports,\" he says.

\"We've been going for 99 years and we want to grow the employment which we offer to the local community.\"

'We voted to take back control'

Sir Bernard Jenkin warns the government to respect the result of the EU referendum

Sir Bernard Jenkin, the MP for Harwich and North Essex, was one of the founders of the Vote Leave campaign in 2015.

He says of the extra paperwork that \"these are barriers which the EU has erected even though we have agreed a free trade deal\".

He adds: \"If we sign up to this [proposed] deal we're going to be re-subjugating all food and agricultural production in the UK to EU rules, when in the referendum we voted to take back control.\"

He says he has \"great sympathy for shellfish producers and people who sell sausages into the EU\", but says those sorts of businesses make up only a small part of the economy.

Figures from the House of Commons library show that 41% of British exports went to the EU in 2025. The figure has fluctuated between 41% and 44% for the past 10 years.

But exports of goods which include foodstuffs to the EU have fallen by 14% since 2019, while services – which are people-based, involving things such as finance or research – have increased by 28%.

\"I recognise that it's been tough for some exporters to the EU but the growth of the economy is far, far bigger than sausages and shellfish,\" says Sir Bernard.

\"Their contribution is minute compared with the whole economy, which is much more service sector-orientated and much more geared to exporting to the rest of the world than it is to the EU.

\"We will do better outside the EU. We should stay outside the EU and the government should respect the referendum decision and not put up taxes in order to pay more contributions to the EU.\"
